clinicalPearls: A congenital, usually unilateral, greyish oval or round excavation of the optic disc, most often located in the inferotemporal quadrant.
Discs harbouring a pit are frequently larger than normal, and the pit may be accompanied by a peripapillary crescent or halo.
The major sight-threatening complication is optic disc pit maculopathy, a serous macular detachment often with an inner and outer retinoschisis-like separation.
Fluid in maculopathy is thought to originate from vitreous or cerebrospinal fluid tracking through the pit rather than from a classic RPE leak.
Fluorescein angiography typically shows late hyperfluorescence of the pit but, importantly, no active leakage into the subretinal fluid.
Optical coherence tomography is the key investigation, demonstrating schisis-like intraretinal splitting and subretinal fluid communicating with the pit.
Temporal pits are more likely to develop maculopathy than nasal or central pits.
Vitrectomy with gas tamponade, sometimes combined with internal limiting membrane peel or laser to the temporal disc margin, is the mainstay for persistent maculopathy.
reference.pathophysiology: An optic disc pit represents a localised herniation of dysplastic retina into a defect in the lamina cribrosa, regarded as part of the optic disc coloboma spectrum arising from imperfect closure of the fetal fissure. The pit is a discontinuity in the normal disc architecture through which the subarachnoid space and vitreous cavity may communicate with the intraretinal and subretinal spaces. In optic pit maculopathy, fluid, believed to derive from liquefied vitreous or cerebrospinal fluid, tracks through the pit and dissects into the retina, producing a schisis-like inner separation and an overlying serous detachment. Persistent traction and fluid accumulation lead to photoreceptor damage and progressive central visual loss.
additionalDifferentials: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment involving the macula
Glaucomatous acquired pit of the optic nerve
additionalInvestigations: Optical coherence tomography of the macula and optic nerve head
Fundus fluorescein angiography to exclude active RPE leakage
Automated perimetry for arcuate or centrocaecal field defects
Fundus autofluorescence to map the extent of serous detachment
Serial fundus photography to monitor pit and maculopathy
OCT angiography to exclude a secondary choroidal neovascular membrane
redFlags: New central metamorphopsia or blurring indicating evolving maculopathy
Progressive serous macular detachment on serial OCT
Marked reduction in best-corrected visual acuity
Features suggesting acquired glaucomatous pitting with raised intraocular pressure
reference.prognosis: An isolated pit without maculopathy is compatible with normal lifelong vision. Once maculopathy develops, untreated cases frequently progress to poor central acuity, though surgical repair can restore useful vision in a substantial proportion.
pitfalls: Mistaking optic pit maculopathy for central serous chorioretinopathy and delaying appropriate surgical referral.
Assuming subretinal fluid arises from an RPE leak; fluorescein typically shows no active leak, misleading the unwary.
Confusing a congenital pit with an acquired glaucomatous pit and missing coexisting raised intraocular pressure.
Underestimating the chronicity of maculopathy fluid, which may resorb slowly even after successful surgery.
